blueprint

/BLOO-print/ - the stress falls on BLOO · noun

Hear It

What It Means

A blueprint is a detailed plan that specifies exactly how something will be built or carried out.

Volunteers followed the barn-raising blueprint so faithfully that the frame stood by dusk without a single wasted cut.

Example

When Coach Odom's tiny school somehow produced three straight championship relay teams, rival coaches began asking for her blueprint — and she handed it over freely: a binder that mapped every practice to the minute, every drill to a stopwatch split, every taper to the calendar's final week. Copy it all you like, she warned; the binder builds the season, but you still have to supply the runners.

Blueprint is the right word because the binder doesn't merely gesture at a philosophy — it specifies the whole construction, down to minutes and splits, exactly the way a builder's drawing fixes every joint before the first nail. Note the word's honest limit, too, and Odom names it: a blueprint tells you precisely how to build the thing, never whether your materials can bear it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

schematic: A schematic is the technician's diagram — it maps how a circuit's parts connect, all symbols and lines. A blueprint covers the whole build, dimensions included, from foundation to roofline.

roadmap: A roadmap sequences a plan's stages over time — what happens first, next, and last. A blueprint specifies the finished thing itself: not when the parts arrive, but exactly how they fit.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

guesswork: proceeding with no worked-out design

improvisation: building it as you go

Where it sits · how completely the plan pins down the result

outline → blueprint → specification

outline vs. blueprint: An outline is looser than a blueprint: it names the plan's big pieces in order and stops, while a blueprint dictates dimensions, materials, and how every part joins.

specification vs. blueprint: Specification goes further than blueprint — a blueprint governs one build, while a specification sets exact tolerances that every builder, in every factory, must reproduce.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — blue: the color of the copied page (from the cyanotype process)

Root — print: a pressed or reproduced mark (Latin premere, "to press")

Put it together: Blue + print = the blue page. Nineteenth-century builders copied their drawings by a chemical process that turned the paper deep blue and left the lines white — a blueprint was literally the blue print of the master drawing. The color faded out of the technology; the meaning of a complete, buildable plan stayed. Print itself is Latin premere, "to press," and English presses it into service everywhere.

Use the root in a new word: imprint: The museum's prize fossil preserves the imprint of a fern that pressed into soft mud four hundred million years ago.

Root Check

Word Choice

concrete / architectural

Blueprint keeps its hard hat even in figurative use: call a policy a blueprint and you are promising specifics — parts, order, measurements. If the plan only names stages and dates, roadmap is the honest word; if it only sketches intentions, don't dress it in drafting paper. This unit's methodical worker is exactly who a blueprint is written for.
